mcq.q: How do Risko and Gilbert (2016) define cognitive offloading?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Memorizing a great deal of information so that no outside tools are needed when doing a task
The use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task
Splitting a task into many steps so that other people do each step one after another
Resting between work sessions so that memory recovers and remembers things better
mcq.e: The paper: "the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand."

mcq.q: Which example does the paper give of cognitive offloading?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Tilting the head to perceive a rotated image, or programming a phone to remind you of an upcoming appointment
Reading a lesson aloud many times to remember it faster before walking into the exam room
Memorizing friends' phone numbers so that they need not be stored in the phone's contacts
Closing the eyes to concentrate on a hard problem or counting silently from one to a hundred
mcq.e: The opening: "If you have ever tilted your head to perceive a rotated image, or programmed a smartphone to remind you of an upcoming appointment, you have engaged in cognitive offloading".

mcq.q: Why does cognitive offloading help people?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: It makes every task reach maximum performance whatever the ability of the tool used
It lets the brain rest completely so that brain areas do not have to work during a task
It helps overcome capacity limits, minimize computational effort
It lets people avoid learning any new skill at all for the whole of their lives
mcq.e: The paper: "Offloading cognition helps us to overcome such capacity limitations, minimize computational effort, and achieve cognitive feats that would not otherwise be possible."

mcq.q: In which domains has cognitive offloading been shown to improve performance?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Only long-term memory, with no other domain demonstrated in the paper
Only language and reading comprehension, with no other domain mentioned
Perception, memory, arithmetic, counting and spatial reasoning
Only arithmetic, with no other domain demonstrated in the paper
mcq.e: The paper: "cognitive offloading has been demonstrated to improve performance across several domains (e.g., perception, memory, arithmetic, counting, and spatial reasoning)".

mcq.q: What does the paper say about the history of offloading?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: It is ancient (finger counting, abacuses, knotted quipus)
It is entirely new, appearing only with computers and the Internet in the last few decades
It has been studied systematically for hundreds of years by philosophers
It exists only in modern humans and has no history in ancient societies
mcq.e: The paper: "the phenomenon it refers to is ancient (e.g., finger-counting and abacuses in numerical cognition, systems of knots or quipus for memory)" but "has rarely been the target of systematic experimental investigation in and of itself."

mcq.q: What are the two kinds of offloading by where the load goes?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Into long-term memory and into short-term memory of the very person doing the task
Onto the body (such as head tilts, gestures) and into the world (such as writing, typing
Onto the teacher and onto classmates when help is needed while doing the task
Onto easy tasks and onto hard tasks depending on the difficulty of the task
mcq.e: The paper: "actions that offload cognitive demands onto-the-body and into-the-world".

mcq.q: What is external normalization?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Using an external reminder to trigger an intention that will be carried out later on
Using physical action such as head tilting to align a stimulus with a representation stored in memory
Using an Internet search engine to look up information not yet known when facing a hard question
Using internal mental rotation to align a stimulus with a representation stored in memory
mcq.e: Glossary: "External normalization: the use of physical action (e.g., head tilt) to align a stimulus with a representation stored in memory."

mcq.q: What is internal normalization?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Tilting the head to align the orientation of a stimulus with a representation in long-term memory
Writing on paper so as not to keep information in the head during a complex task
Creating an external cue to trigger a delayed intention at the appropriate time
An internal transformation (such as mental rotation) that aligns a stimulus representation with one stored in memory
mcq.e: Glossary: "Internal normalization: use of internal transformation (i.e., mental rotation) to align an internal representation of a stimulus with a representation stored in memory."

mcq.q: What drives spontaneous head tilting according to the paper?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Only the color of the words on the screen decides whether people tilt their heads
Internal demand (rotation cost): the more disoriented the display or the more items
Only the length of each word decides whether people tilt their heads while reading
Nothing decides it, because head tilting always occurs completely at random
mcq.e: The paper: "individuals are more likely to spontaneously physically rotate as the display becomes more disoriented or as the number of items in the display increases... as the internal demands... increase, the likelihood of spontaneous external normalization also increases."

mcq.q: Why are internal demand and offloading called "dissociable"?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Because internal demand is always zero in every condition, so it cannot predict offloading
When both words and frame rotate versus only words, costs and physiological demand are similar
Because offloading occurs only when internal demand is zero in every experimental condition
Because internal demand has never been measured in any study of offloading
mcq.e: The paper: the two conditions "yield similar rotation costs and similar responses on a physiological measure of demand. Nevertheless, spontaneous rates of external normalization are much higher when both the words and the frame are rotated".

mcq.q: How does the paper explain that dissociation?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: People deliberately slow down to be accurate, so rotation cost does not reflect true effort
People rely on an erroneous metacognitive evaluation of demand
People always tilt their heads out of habit and are not influenced by any evaluation
People cannot see the frame of the display, so they cannot decide whether to rotate
mcq.e: The paper: "individuals rely on an erroneous metacognitive evaluation of demand... individuals incorrectly report that rotated word and frame displays are more time-consuming and error-prone, and judge these displays to be more effortful to read".

mcq.q: What is intention offloading?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Handing every decision about one's actions over to other people to carry out
Saving a document's content in the computer so that it can be looked up in the future
Creating cues in the environment to trigger a delayed intention
Keeping all one's intentions by rehearsing them continually in one's head
mcq.e: Glossary: "Intention offloading: creation of a cue in the external environment to trigger a delayed intention."

mcq.q: What is prospective memory?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: The ability to remember the location of familiar objects at home or at work
The ability to recall past events accurately and completely
The ability to predict the outcome of an action before carrying it out
The ability to remember to carry out intended actions in the future
mcq.e: The paper: "Our ability to remember delayed intentions is termed 'prospective memory'".

mcq.q: Why is prospective memory often supported by external tools?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Because intentions are always too long to hold completely in the head
Because humans have no ability to remember intentions in any circumstances
Because external tools are always more accurate than any human memory
Intentions are often not triggered by perceptual cues
mcq.e: The paper: "in many cases, our intentions are not effectively triggered by perceptual cues in our environment, and therefore action must be self-initiated... people have long supported prospective memory by using external tools to supply perceptual cues".

mcq.q: Which factors increase intention offloading (setting reminders)?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Complete belief that one's memory is better than any external tool
Increased memory load or interruptions
Plenty of free time and no one disturbing the person during the task
A very simple task that the person has been used to for many years
mcq.e: The paper: "Individuals are more likely to offload intentions when their memory load increases or when they encounter interruptions; both these factors impair performance when offloading is prevented."

mcq.q: What did people with lower memory confidence do in the intention offloading task?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: They set no reminders because they distrust any outside tool
They set the same number of reminders whatever their confidence
They set fewer reminders because they think reminders do not work for them
They set more reminders, even after controlling for objective ability
mcq.e: The paper: "Individuals with lower confidence in their memory abilities were more likely to spontaneously set reminders, even after controlling for any influence of objective ability".

mcq.q: Is the link between confidence and intention offloading domain-general?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Yes; people less confident in perceptual judgments also set more reminders in the intention offloading task
No; confidence has no relation to setting reminders in any domain
No; only confidence in memory relates to setting reminders in the task
Yes; but only in people who have previously suffered brain injury
mcq.e: The paper: "this relation with metacognitive confidence is domain-general. When individuals performed a separate perceptual judgment task... individuals with lower confidence in their perceptual judgments set more reminders in the intention offloading task."

mcq.q: What is a salient benefit of offloading intentions into the environment?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Offloaded representations may be more durable and less prone to distortion
External reminders always fire at exactly the right time, so intentions never fail
The person no longer needs to remember having set a reminder, so no extra effort is spent
External reminders make people forget the goals they had set altogether
mcq.e: The paper: "offloaded representations may be more durable and less prone to distortion than those stored internally, leading to an increased likelihood of intention fulfillment".

mcq.q: In the short-term memory task, how often did participants write items down when they needed to remember only 2?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: About 4% of the time, since performance was already at ceiling without offloading
About 100% of the time, since they did not trust their memory with only two items
About 40% of the time, even though performance was already at ceiling without offloading
About 0% of the time, since two items are too few for anyone to write down
mcq.e: The paper: "did so about 40% of the time when they were required to remember only two items, a memory load at which performance was already at ceiling without offloading."

mcq.q: What is notable about writing when remembering only 2 items?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Participants correctly judged offloading would not help but did it anyway out of habit
Participants erroneously judged that offloading would improve their performance in this condition
Participants always found that writing slowed and worsened them, so wrote only when forced
Participants did not even realize they were writing the items down while working
mcq.e: The paper: "Crucially, individuals erroneously judged that offloading would improve their performance in this latter condition."

mcq.q: What three explanations are given for superfluous offloading?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: An undetected benefit, a bias against cognitive effort, and an erroneous metacognitive belief
Very poor memory, too little practice time, and no guidance from experienced people
Fear of low marks, fear of criticism, and fear of having to redo the task again
Curiosity about the tool, pressure from observers, and a wish to finish the task sooner
mcq.e: The paper: "(i) an undetected performance benefit (ii) a bias against cognitive effort (Box 2), and/or (iii) an erroneous metacognitive belief that the offloading will in fact benefit performance."

mcq.q: What is the "choice/no choice" paradigm?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Some questions allow free-form answers while others allow only true or false
Some tasks are chosen by participants while others are preselected by the experimenter
Some conditions oblige a particular strategy while others let participants freely choose among available strategies
Some participants are paid while others are not paid for taking part
mcq.e: Box 1: "in some conditions participants are obliged (i.e., they have no choice) to employ a particular strategy and in others they are free (i.e., they have the choice) to select among a set of available strategies."

mcq.q: What does the "no choice–internal" condition measure?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Performance when the person can rely only on internal memory, unable to store information externally
Performance when the person must store information externally on paper or a computer
Satisfaction of the person with strategies for storing information inside the head
Spontaneous offloading when the person may choose freely between internal and external storage
mcq.e: Box 1: "No Choice–Internal: Individuals are tasked with remembering a given piece of information without being able to store it externally. This condition provides a measure of performance when the individual has to rely solely on their internal memory."

mcq.q: What does the "choice" condition measure?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Performance when people are forced to use only their own internal memory
The difficulty of the task when the amount of information to remember is doubled
Spontaneous offloading when people freely choose between storing internally and externally
Performance when people are forced to store all information on an external device
mcq.e: Box 1: "Choice: Participants are allowed to freely choose between storing information internally or externally. This condition provides a measure of the spontaneous offloading of memory demands".

mcq.q: What is one challenge of the choice/no choice paradigm?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: It cannot be used for memory and can be used only for perceptual tasks
It is so costly that it can be applied only with groups of thousands of participants
Obliging a strategy may be ineffective, and may add load from having to inhibit a preferred strategy
It always gives the same result whether participants are given a choice or are forced
mcq.e: Box 1: "attempting to oblige individuals to adopt a strategy might not be effective in some circumstances. In addition, forcing individuals to use a particular strategy could introduce demands associated with being required to inhibit the use of another possibly preferred strategy."

mcq.q: What two opposed views on effort bias does Box 2 present?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: Cognitive impartiality (no bias about type of effort)
A bias toward modern tools and a bias toward traditional tools among people
A bias toward easy tasks and a bias toward hard tasks in human beings
A bias against physical effort and a bias against social effort in the person
mcq.e: Box 2: "On the cognitive impartiality view the cognitive system has no bias or is indifferent to the type of effort required... An alternative view, which might be called the 'cognitive miser' view, is that individuals have an inherent bias against expending cognitive effort."

mcq.q: According to the "soft constraints" hypothesis, what determines the preferred solution?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: The opinion of the people nearby about the solution the person is weighing
The accuracy of the solution, with the most accurate always preferred
The amount of time required, not the type of effort; the faster solution is preferred
The type of effort required, with cognitive effort always avoided more than motor effort
mcq.e: Box 2: "according to the soft constraints hypothesis, it is not the type of effort but rather the amount of time required that determines the preferred solution (i.e., the solution with the shorter time being the preferred one)."

mcq.q: What is the "minimal memory" view?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the concept
o: The cognitive system has no bias and is completely neutral to every type of effort
The cognitive system is biased toward using as much memory as possible to avoid outside tools
The cognitive system is biased toward minimizing memory demands, even at higher perceptual-motor cost
The cognitive system always picks the solution with the shortest total time
mcq.e: Box 2: "the 'minimal memory' view, according to which the cognitive system is biased toward minimizing demands on memory (even in the face of potentially greater perceptual-motor costs)."

mcq.q: What is a transactive memory system?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: A memory system in which everyone remembers exactly the same information in a group
A memory system in which knowledge is distributed across two or more individuals
An artificial memory system that completely replaces natural human memory at work
A memory system that exists only inside one person's brain and has no link to others
mcq.e: The paper: "knowledge is distributed across two or more individuals such that the system as a whole knows more than any one individual"; glossary: "a memory system composed of a group that collectively encodes, stores, and retrieves knowledge."

mcq.q: Where has recent research extended transactive memory?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: To human-technology systems, such as computers and the Internet
To systems among generations within the same family over many years
To systems among nerve cells in the same region of the brain
To systems among different animal species living in the same area
mcq.e: The paper: "extended this notion of socially distributed memory to human-technology transactive memory systems".

mcq.q: What is the defining attribute of a transactive memory system?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: A shift from remembering "when" to remembering "why" information appeared
A shift from remembering "who" to remembering "how much" information was saved
A shift from remembering "where" to remembering "when" information appeared
A shift from remembering "what" to remembering "where"
mcq.e: The paper: "a defining attribute of a transactive memory system is a shift from remembering 'what' to remembering 'where'."

mcq.q: What does the meeting-file example illustrate?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: After saving a meeting's content to a file, you need not remember the content
After saving a meeting's content to a file, you remember both content and location better
After saving a meeting's content to a file, you always forget even that there was a meeting
After saving a meeting's content to a file, you need not remember anything about it at all
mcq.e: The paper: "when you offload information about a meeting to a file on your computer, you no longer need to remember the content of the file, but you do need to remember where to find it."

mcq.q: What did saving an initial word list do for memory of a second list?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: It reduced memory for the second list because the brain was overloaded
It enhanced memory for the second list by reducing proactive interference
It had no effect on memory for the second list
It made people forget both lists after a while
mcq.e: The paper: "when individuals saved an initial list of words it enhanced memory for a second list [35]. The authors argued that saving reduced the likelihood that the first list of words interfered with memory for the second (i.e., reduced proactive interference)".

mcq.q: What does the paper say about online searching and metacognition?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Searching online always makes people underestimate their own knowledge
Searching online lets people know exactly what they do and do not know
Searching online has no effect on how people evaluate themselves
Searching for information about one topic can make people believe they have more knowledge "in the head" about another topic
mcq.e: The paper: "searching for information online about one topic can lead individuals to believe that they have more knowledge 'in-the-head' and generate more 'brain activity' when answering questions about another topic".

mcq.q: What did people who recently used Google on a quiz tend to do afterwards?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Refused to take the next quiz because they felt unable to do it without the Internet
Reported unchanged self-esteem and predicted their score accurately on the next quiz
Reported higher cognitive self-esteem and predicted better performance on the next quiz even without help
Reported lower cognitive self-esteem and predicted worse performance on the next quiz
mcq.e: The paper: "individuals who had recently used Google to help them complete a quiz reported higher levels of cognitive self-esteem. They also predicted that they would do better on a subsequent quiz, even without help from external resources".

mcq.q: How did people react to general-knowledge questions when they knew they could look answers up afterward?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: They answered more accurately because they were reassured they could check later
They said "don't know" less often and reported higher feeling-of-knowing than without the Internet
They refused to answer any general-knowledge question, trusting the Internet to answer
They were more likely to say "don't know" and reported lower feeling-of-knowing
mcq.e: The paper: "when they knew they would subsequently have access to the internet, participants were more likely to answer 'don't know' and reported lower feeling-of-knowing to the trivia questions [52]."

mcq.q: In the GPS study of Box 3, how did those who followed turn-by-turn directions do when driving the route again without aid?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: The same as the other group since both had driven the route before
They could not drive again because they had forgotten the route completely
Worse, although the first time they outperformed the no-aid group
Better than the other group because they had learned the route from the aided drive
mcq.e: Box 3: "individuals who drove a predetermined route using a turn-by-turn navigation system outperformed individuals who had no aid. However, individuals in the former group had poorer memory for scenes from the route and, when asked to drive the route a second time without an aid, performed more poorly".

mcq.q: What did the photography study show about memory?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Photographing had no effect on memory for the object a day after it was taken
Photographing an object improved memory for it a day later, most of all if the whole object was photographed
Photographing an object impaired memory for it a day later, and photographing only part of it reduced the cost
Photographing impaired memory only if the photographer knew the photo would be viewed again
mcq.e: Box 3: "Memory for the objects tested a day later revealed impaired memory for the photographed objects. In a subsequent experiment, taking a picture of only part of the object, rather than the whole object, to some extent ameliorated this cost".

mcq.q: What is notable about the photography study?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Participants were sure they would see the pictures again during the memory test
Participants had to delete the pictures right after taking them to avoid copying
Participants used professional cameras so the pictures were always very detailed
Participants did not necessarily expect the pictures during the memory test
mcq.e: Box 3: "individuals did not necessarily expect to have the pictures available during the memory test. Thus, the de-prioritization of information that is potentially available externally might occur spontaneously".

mcq.q: What is "automation complacency"?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Uncritical reliance on the output of an automated decision aid
The decision to offload always being made actively and consciously by the user
Failure to be sufficiently vigilant regarding the performance of automated processes
Gradual deterioration of a developed skill from lack of use over a long time
mcq.e: Box 3: "'automation complacency', the failure to be sufficiently vigilant with respect to the performance of automated processes".

mcq.q: What is "automation bias"?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: The tendency to uncritically rely on the output of an automated decision aid
Deterioration of a developed skill because it has not been practiced for long
Bias in an automated tool when giving results to different groups of users
Insufficient vigilance toward processes that have been fully automated
mcq.e: Box 3: "'automation bias', the tendency to uncritically rely on the output of an automated decision aid".

mcq.q: What is "skill decay"?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Users forgetting the passwords of the automated devices they use
New skills being impossible to develop when the learner is very young
Deterioration of a developed ability over time from long-term reliance on automated processes
Automated tools working worse and worse after many years of continuous use
mcq.e: Box 3: "The long-term reliance on automated processes could also lead to cognitive 'skill decay' where a developed ability deteriorates over time".

mcq.q: What does the highly automated vehicle example show about automation's effects?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: transactive memory and costs
o: Highly automated driving always improves situation awareness whatever the driver does
Highly automated driving always reduces situation awareness whatever the driver does
Effects depend on how freed resources are allocated: situation awareness improves if attention goes to the environment, worsens if devoted to unrelated tasks
Highly automated driving has no effect on the driver's situation awareness
mcq.e: Box 3: "driving a highly automated vehicle can improve situation awareness relative to manual driving if individuals are motivated to attend to the environment, but can impair it if they decide to devote 'freed resources' to driving-unrelated tasks".

mcq.q: How does the paper's metacognitive framework treat offloading?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: As an automatic reflex that never involves any evaluation or choice by the person
As a strategy chosen after a strategy-selection phase influenced by metacognitive evaluation of internal and "extended" options
As a decision made by others on the user's behalf without the user knowing
As a behavior occurring only when the outside tool is proven perfectly accurate
mcq.e: The paper: "offloading represents a type of strategy to achieve some cognitive goal, and follows a strategy-selection phase... influenced by a metacognitive evaluation of the available options (arrow A)".

mcq.q: What does arrow A in Figure 3 represent?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: Metacognitive evaluation of internal and extended strategies influencing strategy selection
The external tool updating itself to fit each user's needs
Offloading directly affecting lower-level cognitive processes such as memory
Use of a strategy altering the user's later metacognitive evaluations
mcq.e: Caption of Figure 3: "selecting between offloading and relying on internal processes is influenced by metacognitive evaluations... (arrow A)".

mcq.q: What does arrow B represent?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: The outside tool influencing how fast the user processes information
Metacognitive evaluation determining which strategy is chosen next time
Engaging in internal or extended strategies changes later metacognitive evaluations
Offloading directly affecting lower-level cognitive processes such as memory
mcq.e: Caption: "engaging in either internal or extended strategies can influence subsequent metacognitive evaluations (arrow B)... after successful use of a GPS system we may come to believe that it is a more reliable guide than our unaided memory."

mcq.q: What does arrow C represent?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: Offloading directly affects lower-level cognitive processes
Metacognitive evaluation changing how the user picks tools next time
The outside tool adjusting itself to compensate for the user's cognitive decline
Extended strategies being chosen based on beliefs about tool reliability
mcq.e: Caption: "Offloading can also directly impact on our lower-level cognitive processes (arrow C). An example of this would be a reduction in our internal spatial memory for a location after reliance on GPS navigation."

mcq.q: Why does the model predict a "self-reinforcing loop" with GPS?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: Because GPS is always accurate, so the user never needs memory again
Because users always remember the route after using GPS once
Because the GPS maker requires users to use the device whenever they travel
Offloading reduces internal memory and confidence (C and B)
mcq.e: The paper: "The tendency to offload wayfinding to the more accurate GPS will likely reduce both our internal spatial memory... (arrow C) and our metacognitive confidence in it (arrow B), which will in turn increase the likelihood that we choose to rely on the external artefact in the future (arrow A)."

mcq.q: What does the Inuit wayfinding example illustrate?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: A drift away from reliance on internal capabilities in an environment with effective cognitive technologies
That the Inuit never use outside tools for navigating
That the Inuit fully reject modern technology in daily life
That the Inuit have better spatial memory than every other community in every setting
mcq.e: The paper: "a drift away from reliance on internal capabilities when situated in an environment with effective cognitive technologies ([68] for an example of this type of drift in the context of Inuit wayfinding)."

mcq.q: Is the decision to offload necessarily a conscious one?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: No; the strategy-selection phase does not imply awareness of choosing (for example gesture often occurs unaware)
No; but only for young children, since adults always offload consciously
Yes; if people are not aware, the behavior does not count as offloading
Yes; every act of offloading needs conscious deliberation and an explicit choice
mcq.e: The paper: "the strategy-selection phase postulated above does not necessarily imply that individuals are aware of making a choice... gesture... can occur without individuals necessarily being aware of it."

mcq.q: Which two practical implications does the paper highlight?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: Offloading has applications only in industry and none in education
People with impaired unaided cognition may benefit especially from offloading
Offloading benefits only healthy people and always harms people with cognitive impairment
Offloading has applications only for children and none for older adults
mcq.e: The paper: "First, individuals with impaired unaided cognitive ability may particularly benefit from cognitive offloading... The second general area... is education".

mcq.q: How does gesture help children learn in education?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: By fully replacing the teacher's spoken explanation in every subject in class
By "lightening the load", a benefit that appears to outstrip offloading onto external manipulatives
By working only with young children and losing all effect as they grow a little
By raising cognitive load so children must try harder and remember better
mcq.e: The paper: "gesture helps children learn by 'lightening the load' [11] and, interestingly, this benefit appears to outstrip that garnered by offloading demands onto external manipulatives [77]."

mcq.q: What is the key condition for offloading to benefit learning?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: The offloaded demand must be unnecessary for the learning goal
The offloaded demand should be picked randomly by learners without considering anything else
The offloaded demand should be as much as possible so learners have plenty of rest afterwards
The offloaded demand must be the most important part of the learning goal so learners need not do it
mcq.e: The paper: "any benefit of offloading will be contingent on the fact that the demand being offloaded is unnecessary with respect to the learning goal... it is important that what is 'saved' by offloading is redistributed productively rather than being re-allocated to superfluous activities".

mcq.q: Which load distinctions does the paper reference?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: Short-term load, long-term load and medium-term load in a course
Teacher load, student load and parent load in the teaching process
Physical load, emotional load and social load in learning activities
Necessary/intrinsic/germane load versus unnecessary/extraneous load
mcq.e: The paper: "see [78] for relevant distinctions between necessary/intrinsic/germane load and unnecessary/extraneous load in learning" (links to Module 02).

mcq.q: What long-term open question does the paper raise?
mcq.sec: Risko and Gilbert 2016: the framework and implications
o: Whether extended offloading makes search engines work better over time
How extended offloading affects unaided ability ("does Google make us stupid?")
Whether extended offloading lowers the cost of technology purchases for users
Whether extended offloading raises the number of Internet users worldwide

mcq.q: What is the central claim of Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011)?

essay.q: State the definition of cognitive offloading and the two triggering mechanisms (internal demand and metacognitive evaluation) in Risko and Gilbert (2016). Give evidence for each.
essay.m: Hint: Definition: using physical action to reduce cognitive demand. Internal demand: the more disoriented the display or the more items, the more head tilting; higher memory load or interruptions lead to more reminders. Metacognition: word-and-frame versus word rotation have similar costs but more tilting because of misjudged demand; less confident people set more reminders; writing about 40% of the time with only 2 items.

essay.q: Describe the four experiments of Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) and the conclusion about the "Google effect". Give two limits on generalizing to learning with AI.
essay.m: Hint: Experiment 1 primes the concept of computers after hard questions (712 versus 591 ms); 2: believing erasure gives better recall (0.31 and 0.29 versus 0.22 and 0.19); 3: content recall best when believing erasure (0.93), saved items recognized more accurately; 4: location recall (0.49) beats statement recall (0.23). Conclusion: remembering "where" rather than "what". Limits: trivia and lookup, not structured learning; a cue existed for the folder; no generative AI.

essay.q: Explain the metacognitive framework of offloading (arrows A, B, C) and the self-reinforcing loop. Apply it to a programming student who uses AI to write code.
essay.m: Hint: A: metacognitive evaluation selects the strategy; B: using a strategy alters evaluation; C: offloading affects lower-level cognition. GPS example. Application (design inference): the student sees the AI writes code better than they do so offloads (A); with few attempts confidence falls (B) and debugging skill weakens (C); next time they offload more. Measure: AI queries, confidence, no-AI scores.

essay.q: Analyze the evidence on generative AI and critical thinking in Lee (2025), Gerlich (2025) and Kosmyna (2025): design, main results and limits of each.
essay.m: Hint: Lee: 319 people, 936 examples; high confidence in AI goes with less critical thinking, high self-confidence with more; self-report. Gerlich: 666 people, r = −0.68 and −0.75, partial mediation (−0.25 of −0.42); cross-sectional, self-report, convenience sample. Kosmyna: 54 people, EEG; 83.3% versus 11.1% could not quote; preprint, small sample, one LLM, essay writing. None proves solid causation.

essay.q: Propose how to measure "superfluous offloading" and skill with AI removed in your thesis, based on Risko and Gilbert and Kosmyna, with limitations.
essay.m: Hint: An AI-removed session (like session 4): a no-AI test; ask students to quote or re-explain the work they just did; log AI queries (frequency, type); confidence before the test (Modules 05, 06); separate extraneous load from load tied to the learning goal. Limits: small sample, one AI tool, practice effects between sessions, self-report; needs comparison groups (Module 13).

essay.q: Why does Gerlich, with strong correlations (r = −0.68 to −0.75), still not justify concluding "AI reduces critical thinking"? Give three alternative explanations and how to test them.
essay.m: Hint: Cross-sectional, self-report, convenience sample from social media. Alternatives: people with low critical thinking choose to use AI more (reverse causation); a third factor such as age, education or occupation; measurement bias (heavy AI users rate themselves differently). Tests: repeated measures over time, experiments manipulating AI use, controlling confounders, and measuring critical thinking with a standardized test rather than self-report.
